cues.text: A Priest's Secret Fear
In 1378, amid the confusion of the Western Schism, French cardinals elected the antipope Clement VII in opposition to Rome-recognized Pope Urban VI.
The resulting uncertainty over which bishops held valid authority left many priests across Western Europe unsure whether their own ordinations were canonically sound.
Father Mosen Jaime Carros was a parish priest in Moncada, near Valencia, and had been ordained by a bishop appointed under Clement VII's obedience.
He lived for years in genuine anguish that every Mass he offered and every sacrament he administered might be invalid.
Christmas at Moncada
On Christmas Day 1392, a woman named Angela Alpicat brought her five-year-old daughter Ines to Mass at Moncada.

At the moment of the elevation, the child insisted she saw a beautiful infant cradled in the priest's hands, and after Mass she refused to leave the church, wanting to stay and play with the child she had seen.
The following day Father Carros, wanting to test what the girl had described, took two hosts to the altar but consecrated only one.
A Child's Answer
Elevating first the consecrated host and then the unconsecrated one, the priest asked Ines what she saw in each.
Of the consecrated host she answered simply, 'I see Baby Jesus'; of the other, she said there was nothing there at all.

The distinction, made without hesitation by a child too young to have any concept of the schism troubling her priest, dissolved the anguish Father Carros had carried for years over the validity of his own ordination.
A Recognized Local Tradition

The event is recorded in Father Odorico Raynaldi's Annales Ecclesiastici and preserved in numerous documents in the municipal archives of Moncada, and has been kept as a local devotional tradition in the region ever since.

Ines herself is remembered locally as the Venerable Ines de Moncada, who is said to have spent the rest of her life as a hermit and penitent in a cave known as El Rodeno, still a site of pilgrimage today.
Legacy

The Moncada account belongs to a distinct and recurring category of Eucharistic account — not a physical transformation of the host itself, but a vision granted to resolve a real crisis of conscience within the Church.
Whatever one makes of the precise historicity of a five-year-old's testimony six centuries removed, the story has endured in Moncada.

It serves as a reminder that the schism-era Church's deepest anxieties about sacramental validity were, in the popular imagination at least, answered not by a council or a theologian but by a child's unguarded honesty.
